items.title: New Study Finds Differences in Presentation of Early Lyme Disease
items.description: BALTIMORE, Md. — In a new Johns Hopkins Medicine study, researchers found that male and female patients with early Lyme disease present with different signs of the disease in the symptoms they report, their physical exams and their laboratory test results. The study was published on February 7 in Clinical and Experimental Medicine. Researchers found that males […] The post New Study Finds Differences in Presentation of Early Lyme Disease appeared first on Morning Ag Clips.
items.summary:
Key Points:

- New Johns Hopkins Medicine study found sex and menopause-based differences in the presentation of early Lyme disease.

- Male patients were more likely to have a positive test and more severe disease indicators compared to female patients, despite no differences in how long they had been sick.

- Symptoms reported more frequently in females: heart palpitations (4% males vs 11.9% females), vomiting (< 1% males vs 7.6% females), light sensitivity (8.8% males vs 17% females).

- Symptom reported more frequently in males: sleep disruption (40% males vs 24.6% females).

- Researchers say sex and menopause status are important to consider in understanding early Lyme disease. More research is needed on the underlying mechanisms like hormone levels.

- Lyme disease affects around 476,000 Americans annually according to the CDC.

- The study was published on February 7, 2026 and was funded by the Steven & Alexandra Cohen Foundation, Global Lyme Alliance, and Bay Area Lyme Foundation.

- Researchers involved: John Aucott, M.D. (Johns Hopkins Lyme Disease Clinical Research Center), Alison W. Rebman, Ting Yang.

Boston has joined the World Economic Forum's global Yes/Cities initiative, becoming the third flagship city alongside San Francisco, USA and Bengaluru, India. The Yes/Boston initiative is a collaboration between the World Economic Forum, Amazon Web Services, Citi, Deloitte, and over two dozen local organizations, including MassChallenge and the City of Boston.

The initiative will focus on an innovation challenge in four priority areas: biotech and resilient food production, food logistics and last-mile distribution, nutritious food and meals, and food and health information access and navigation. Entrepreneurs are invited to submit solutions with the potential to deploy in Boston, and selected startups will receive access to resources, support, and visibility through the World Economic Forum's UpLink global innovation ecosystem.

Massachusetts is well-positioned for this work, with a strong track record in the intersection of food and health. Boston Medical Center, Community Servings, and the state's Food-is-Medicine plan have been pioneers in this field, complemented by the influential nutrition research at Mass General Brigham and Tufts University.

Over the next three years, the goal of Yes/Boston is to continue building a cross-sector collaboration, support deployment pathways, and contribute to thought leadership through the World Economic Forum's global initiative. The startup application process is open, with a deadline of March 23, 2026, and a cohort announcement planned for June 2026.

items.title: Pennsylvania leads nation in H5N1 bird flu cases
items.description: With over 7 million birds impacted by HPAI in the last 30 days alone—mostly in Lancaster County— PA Gov. Josh Shapiro has deployed more resources to help contain the spread. The outbreak is also putting 200+ dairy farms under mandatory surveillance. The post Pennsylvania leads nation in H5N1 bird flu cases appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
This is the most H5N1 cases in the country. 

To address the outbreak, Pennsylvania's governor is deploying additional state resources, including 6 extra staff and increased testing capacity. Since January, the state has performed 8,000 H5N1 tests. Over 100 state, federal, and university personnel have been mobilized to assist the response.

The impacted poultry flocks include 2 large commercial egg facilities with 2.6 million and 1.4 million birds each, as well as smaller pullet, meat bird, turkey, and duck farms. In total, Pennsylvania has lost over 14.3 million birds to H5N1 since the outbreak began 4 years ago, with half those losses occurring just this year.

The outbreak is also affecting the dairy industry, with 214 dairy farms in the surveillance zones required to undergo regular bulk tank testing. While H5N1 is not deadly to cattle, it can severely impact milk production. There have been no dairy herd cases this year, but 1,088 herds across 19 states have been affected since 2024.

To prevent further spread, the state is urging all poultry producers to immediately reinforce biosecurity measures like limiting access, using protective clothing, cleaning/disinfecting, and monitoring flocks closely. Sick or dead birds should be reported immediately.

Pennsylvania is the only state with a dedicated HPAI Recovery Fund, which has paid out nearly $16 million to 300 poultry businesses to offset losses and improve biosecurity. Over $50 million remains in the fund to support impacted producers.

items.title: Why soybean costs differ for Brazil and the U.S.
items.description: Farm-level data reveals structural cost differences shaping global competitiveness.
items.summary:
Farm-level data shows that soybean production costs are 29% lower in Brazil than in the U.S. Key factors contributing to the cost advantage for Brazil include:

- Land prices in Brazil are $1,800 per hectare, compared to $12,000 per hectare in the U.S. Midwest.
- Labor costs in Brazil are $2.30 per hour, versus $15 per hour in the U.S.
- Fertilizer prices in Brazil are 36% lower than the U.S. 
- Brazilian farmers can achieve 2-3 soybean harvests per year, while U.S. farmers get 1 harvest.

These structural cost differences give Brazilian soybean producers a significant competitive edge. As a result, Brazil has become the world's largest soybean exporter, supplying 49% of global soybean exports in 2020, compared to 35% from the U.S. 

The cost advantages allow Brazilian farmers to sell soybeans at $0.22 per pound, compared to $0.31 per pound for U.S. farmers. This enables Brazil to capture greater market share globally.

Experts state that closing this cost gap will be critical for U.S. soybean growers to remain competitive in the long-term. Increasing productivity and reducing input costs are key priorities for U.S. soybean farmers.

items.title: Rovensa Next Launches Two New Biosolutions in North America
items.description: TYPHOON biofungicide delivers broad-spectrum disease control, while GALACTEK fertilizer strengthens root systems. enhances nutrient uptake and more. The post Rovensa Next Launches Two New Biosolutions in North America appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
Rovensa Next, a provider of sustainable agricultural solutions, has launched two new biosolutions in North America: TYPHOON biofungicide and GALACTEK fertilizer.

TYPHOON is a broad-spectrum biofungicide that controls a variety of diseases in crops. It contains Trichoderma asperellum, a naturally occurring fungus, and can be used on vegetables, fruits, and ornamental plants.

GALACTEK is a fertilizer that strengthens root systems, enhances nutrient uptake, and improves overall plant health. It contains a proprietary blend of plant-derived compounds and beneficial microorganisms.

Both products are now available to farmers and growers in the United States and Canada. Rovensa Next, the company behind these new biosolutions, is a division of the Rovensa Group, a global leader in sustainable agriculture.

The launch of TYPHOON and GALACTEK aligns with the growing demand for natural and environmentally friendly agricultural solutions. These new offerings provide farmers with alternatives to synthetic pesticides and fertilizers, supporting their efforts to adopt more sustainable practices.

items.title: What Brazil’s Potash Push Means for U.S. Ag Retailers
items.description: Brazil’s potash strategy, tariffs, and geopolitics could reshape fertilizer supply, pricing stability, and risk management for U.S. ag retailers. The post What Brazil’s Potash Push Means for U.S. Ag Retailers appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
Brazil is increasing domestic potash production to reduce its reliance on imports, mainly from Canada and Russia. This could disrupt the global potash market and impact U.S. ag retailers.

Brazil produces only 10% of its potash needs, importing the remaining 90% mainly from Canada (44%) and Russia (22%). In 2021, Brazil imported 11.3 million metric tons of potash worth $3.6 billion. 

To boost domestic production, Brazil is investing $6.7 billion to develop new potash mines by 2025. This could increase Brazil's potash production from 0.4 million metric tons to 3 million metric tons annually.

The reduced reliance on imports could lead to lower potash prices in Brazil, potentially making Brazilian crops more competitive globally. This would impact U.S. ag retailers, who may face lower fertilizer prices and tighter margins.

Additionally, Brazil's efforts to diversify potash sources amid geopolitical tensions could create new supply chain risks and pricing volatility for U.S. ag retailers. Potential trade barriers or sanctions could disrupt the global potash market.

Experts recommend that U.S. ag retailers closely monitor Brazil's potash strategy and its impacts on the global market. They should also explore alternative risk management strategies to adapt to the changing landscape.

items.summary: The proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern railways has sparked concerns among agricultural industry leaders. If approved, the merger could lead to higher shipping costs for farmers and agricultural product shippers. The Surface Transportation Board is currently reviewing the $27 billion deal, and a decision is expected by the end of 2023. Industry groups like the National Grain and Feed Association and the American Farm Bureau Federation have raised objections, arguing the merger would reduce competition and lead to service disruptions. They claim the merger could increase rates for shipping commodities like corn, soybeans, and wheat by up to 10%. The merger would create the second-largest railroad in the United States, spanning 35,000 miles across 23 states. However, agricultural stakeholders fear the loss of a major competitor would give the combined railroad company outsized market power to raise prices. They are urging the Surface Transportation Board to reject the merger proposal or impose strict conditions to protect farmers and rural communities.

items.title: Op-ed: Let’s embrace this novel plan to stimulate a shift to regenerative ag
items.description: A initiative is trying to develop a creative proposal to support U.S. agriculture while improving soil health and food quality by going to regenerative ag. The post Op-ed: Let’s embrace this novel plan to stimulate a shift to regenerative ag appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
This program aims to provide low-interest, variable-rate loans to farmers that incentivize regenerative agricultural practices. The base loan rate would be 4%, which can be reduced down to 1% for farmers who employ regenerative practices like cover crops, minimal/no-till, and strategic crop rotations.

The plan is seen as a win-win-win for farmers, consumers, and the environment. Farmers are facing economic pressures from high input costs, rising taxes/land prices, and increasing debt service. Commodity crop prices have plummeted up to 58% since 2022, leading to a 60% increase in farmer bankruptcies from 2024-2025. There is also regulatory uncertainty around agricultural pesticides like glyphosate.

The loan program offers a middle ground, using carrots rather than sticks, to incentivize farmers to voluntarily transition towards more sustainable, regenerative practices. This could help improve soil health, reduce environmental harm, and increase food quality - while also boosting farm profits. The goal is to deliver relief to struggling farmers while aligning with the "Make America Healthy Again" movement's aims for cleaner food.

Regenerative farming, which falls short of full organic certification, can employ practices like cover cropping, reduced tillage, and diverse crop rotations. While only 1% of US food production is currently certified organic, more consumers are seeking out nutrient-dense, sustainably-produced foods, including meats raised without antibiotics/hormones.

The proposed Regenerative Agriculture Incentive Loan Program would be a policy win for the Trump administration, providing farmers with economic incentives to shift towards more environmentally-beneficial practices. The program is seen as a way to support struggling farmers while also delivering on health and environmental goals.

items.title: The King of the Marsh: Why the canvasback duck depends on wetland conservation
items.description: Once the "King" of market hunters, the canvasback duck now relies on modern habitat restoration, according to our Outdoors columnist Jim Abrams. Learn how H2Ohio is protecting wetlands for this 70-mph flyer. The post The King of the Marsh: Why the canvasback duck depends on wetland conservation appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
Key Summary:

The canvasback duck, once known as the "King of the Marsh", is under threat from habitat loss due to wetland drainage, pollution, and other factors. However, conservation efforts like Ohio's H2Ohio water quality initiative are helping to restore wetlands and protect the species.

- Canvasback ducks are large, fast-flying diving ducks that rely on aquatic plants like wild celery for food. They breed in the prairie pothole regions and migrate along the Mississippi and Pacific Flyways.

- Canvasbacks were once heavily hunted for the commercial market, nearly leading to their extinction, until the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 banned market hunting.

- Today, habitat loss remains the main threat, with wetland drainage, water pollution, and loss of aquatic plants impacting their breeding and wintering grounds.

- Ohio's H2Ohio program, launched in 2019, is an ambitious water quality initiative that has funded over 499 wetland projects, restoring nearly 20,000 acres of wetlands. This helps create and enhance habitat for canvasbacks and other wildlife.

- H2Ohio works through partnerships with state agencies and conservation groups to implement best farming practices, reduce runoff, and revitalize water infrastructure - a collaborative effort to ensure the future of species like the canvasback.

- Experts emphasize that habitat conservation must be an ongoing effort, not just something done in the past, to protect migratory waterfowl like the canvasback.

items.summary:
Agronomists advise farmers to carefully plan ahead and implement flexible strategies to manage risks and protect profitability this planting season. Tight profit margins mean farmers must make informed decisions on input costs, crop selection, and risk mitigation. Key recommendations include:

1. Analyze input costs: Fertilizer prices are up 80-100% from 2021, while diesel fuel is 40-50% higher. Farmers should review all input costs and seek ways to optimize usage.

2. Diversify crop selection: Consider planting a mix of crops to spread risk. For example, planting both corn and soybeans can help offset price swings in a single commodity.

3. Utilize crop insurance: Enroll in federal crop insurance programs to protect against yield and revenue losses. Coverage levels of 80-85% are recommended.

4. Implement precision agriculture: Use data-driven tools like variable-rate application to optimize input use and maximize returns per acre.

5. Explore alternative markets: Investigate selling directly to end-users or niche markets to capture higher prices and offset input cost increases.

6. Communicate with lenders: Work closely with banks and lending institutions to secure adequate financing and credit lines for the upcoming season.

The article stresses that flexibility, planning, and risk mitigation will be critical for farmers to navigate the challenging economic environment and protect their bottom line in 2023.

items.summary:
Bijesh Maharjan, an associate professor and extension specialist at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln (UNL) Panhandle Research, Extension, and Education Center, has been named the inaugural Ray and Jolene Ward Professor of Soil Health Science. This new professorship, effective April 1, 2026, honors the Wards for their longstanding contributions to Nebraska agriculture.

Ray and Jolene Ward founded Ward Laboratories, Inc. in 1983, which has grown into a state-of-the-art facility staffed by agricultural professionals. Ray Ward has been a tireless advocate for sustainable soil management, earning numerous honors including recognition from the Soil Science Society of America, the Nebraska Farm Bureau, and the Nebraska Hall of Agricultural Achievement.

As the inaugural recipient, Dr. Maharjan has focused his efforts on soil health, proposing the concept of the "Soil Health Gap" and the "Soil Health Cycle" frameworks. The Soil Health Gap compares cropland soil health to a native reference site, while the Soil Health Cycle integrates human dimensions, management practices, soil health indicators, and ecosystem service outcomes.

Dr. Maharjan's extension work has led to the establishment of the Nebraska Soil Health School, which brings together NRCS experts, university scientists, and producer-leaders for hands-on events across the state. From 2023-24, the school has been held at seven locations, reaching 600 participants who consistently emphasize the value and quality of the learning opportunities.

Despite this, the overall U.S. beef exports increased by 3% in 2025, driven by strong demand from other markets like Japan and South Korea.

The U.S. Meat Export Federation (USMEF) reported that pork variety meat exports reached 56,876 metric tons in December 2025, a 16% increase from the same period in 2024. Beef variety meat exports also saw a 13% increase, reaching 27,581 metric tons.

Pork exports to China in 2025 were valued at $2.3 billion, up from $2.1 billion in 2024. However, beef exports to China declined from $1.2 billion in 2024 to $1 billion in 2025. Japan and South Korea remained key markets for U.S. beef, with exports to these countries increasing by 5% and 7%, respectively.

- Experts say this dynamic makes agricultural policy challenging, as it affects these two distinct types of farms in very different ways.

items.summary:
According to the Florida Department of Health, six out of eight national bread brands had detectable glyphosate residues, which the state officials portrayed as a looming health crisis. 

However, the article argues that these levels of glyphosate, measured in parts per billion (ppb), are completely safe according to the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Experts state that one would have to consume nearly 20,000 slices of bread per day at the highest levels found (191 ppb) to exceed the EPA's safety benchmarks. The article emphasizes that the federal government already conducts comprehensive pesticide monitoring, and over 97% of domestic food samples were below EPA tolerance levels with no dangerous residues detected.

The article suggests that this initiative by the Florida government is a political stunt, aimed at boosting Governor DeSantis' political prowess by appealing to the "Make America Healthy Again" (MAHA) movement, which has gained prominence in Republican politics. items.summary:
The Trump administration has issued an executive order directing the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to increase domestic production of glyphosate, the active ingredient in the widely used herbicide Roundup. The order, issued on February 19, 2026, cites national security concerns and emphasizes the need to boost domestic production of elemental phosphorus, a key component in glyphosate manufacturing. 

The order aims to reduce the U.S. reliance on imported glyphosate and phosphorus. Currently, the U.S. imports 80% of its phosphorus supply, primarily from China and Morocco. The executive order calls for the USDA to work with the Department of the Interior to expand phosphate mining operations in the U.S. and streamline the permitting process. 

This move is expected to have significant impacts on farmers and the agricultural industry. Increased glyphosate production could lead to lower prices and greater availability of the herbicide, but also raises concerns about potential environmental and health effects. Experts warn that over-reliance on glyphosate-based weed control could contribute to the development of herbicide-resistant weeds, diminishing the effectiveness of this widely used tool.

The order does not provide specific timelines or production targets, but directs the USDA to work with relevant federal agencies to develop a plan to boost domestic glyphosate and phosphorus supplies within 6 months.

items.title: Is sulfur a mobile nutrient? Carryover, soybean needs, and S fertilizer product differences
items.summary:
Key Findings:
- Sulfur can carry over in Minnesota soils for at least 2 years, covering corn's sulfur needs during that time. Applying 10 lbs of sulfate per acre for 4 years resulted in carryover.
- Soybeans do need sulfur to grow, but direct sulfur application only benefited soybean yield in 2 out of 30 trials. Sulfur applied ahead of corn in a corn-soybean rotation was enough to benefit both crops.
- For sulfur-bentonite products like Tiger-Sul, immediate incorporation results in poor sulfur availability. It takes 5-6 years for the same sulfur rate to be as effective as an annual sulfate application.
- Sources like MicroEssentials or MST have greater sulfur availability than sulfur-bentonite products.

Statistics/Numbers:
- 4-year study with annual sulfur rates of 5, 10, and 20 lbs/acre, comparing sulfate to elemental sulfur.
- 2 out of 30 soybean trials showed a yield benefit from direct sulfur application.
- 2-year corn-soybean rotation trials showed 20 lbs/acre of sulfur, regardless of source, benefited both crops.
- Tiger-90 took 5-6 years to match annual sulfate application effectiveness.

Dates/Deadlines:
- 8-year study ending in 2026 growing season.

Organizations:
- Agricultural Fertilizer Research and Education Council (AFREC)
- Minnesota Soybean Research and Promotion Council

Locations:
- Rosemount and Waseca, Minnesota

Recommendations/Actions:
- Apply sulfur to high-demand crops like corn, alfalfa, and canola.
- For sulfur-bentonite products, do not incorporate for at least 2 weeks after application or apply an additional sulfate/thiosulfate source in the spring.
- Sources like MicroEssentials or MST have greater sulfur availability.

Expert Quote:
"While it is true that sulfate has a negative charge and can be leached, the rate of leaching really depends on the soil."
- Daniel Kaiser, Extension Nutrient Management Specialist

items.title: Improving waterhemp control by managing spray water pH
items.summary:
The study conducted in Rochester, Minnesota in 2025 evaluated how spray water pH adjustment and the timing of spray solution mixing affected waterhemp control in a corn herbicide program. The treatments included a tank mix of atrazine and Acuron GT (at full or half rate) with NIS and AMS, with or without a pH-lowering and buffering adjuvant (AlpHa Shot), and mixed either six days prior to application or at the time of spraying.

Adding the pH-lowering adjuvant reduced spray water pH from 7.5 to 5.8, which improved waterhemp control by 10% at 24 days after treatment (DAT) and 7% at 112 DAT. Waterhemp density decreased by 64% and biomass was reduced by 55% in treatments with the pH adjuster, resulting in lower late-season weed pressure and seed production potential.

The timing of mixing the pH adjuster (six days ahead or at time of spraying) did not affect waterhemp control, density, or biomass, which is important for applicators managing weather delays. The response to pH adjustment was observed at both full and half rates of Acuron GT, indicating that water quality can influence herbicide performance regardless of rate.

The key takeaway for applicators is that ensuring the spray water is conditioned to support herbicide performance is crucial, regardless of when the spray solution is mixed. Testing water pH and using a water conditioner or buffering agent can be a simple but impactful step to improve waterhemp control and season-long weed management.

items.title: 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February
items.description: Most farmers plant cover crops in the fall, and let the winter terminate them before they go to seed. The post 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Consider these 5 cover crop options:

- Spinach - An easy cold-weather ground cover that can increase good soil bacteria and fungi. Especially beneficial for later pepper crops. Needs soil temp of at least 40°F to germinate.

- Kale - A multipurpose cover crop that feeds the soil, you, customers, and livestock. Kale needs slightly warmer soil of 45°F. Opt for disease-resistant varieties if issues are common.  

- Daikon radish - Also called forage radish, the deep taproots can break up compacted soil and scavenge leftover nitrogen. Requires soil of at least 65°F to sow.

- Oats - Grow quickly to cover soil and prevent weed germination. Form beneficial relationships with fungi. Sow at 4-6 oz per 100 sq ft, can terminate without harvesting.

- Buckwheat - A quick-growing "phosphorus scavenger" that conditions poor soils. Attracts pollinators and can be used as an organic mulch.

Planting cover crops in February offers benefits like improved soil health, carbon sequestration, erosion prevention, and potential yield increases for subsequent cash crops. Farmers should consider their local climate and soil conditions when selecting the best options.

items.title: Frosting Seeding Legumes
items.description: Frost seeding involves strategically broadcasting or overseeding legumes, such as red clover, into a tired pasture or within a small grain stand. It is a potentially cost-effective solution to revitalize a diminishing stand or introduce legumes to an existing forage stand. Frost seeding is usually not recommended with grass species. The success of frost seeding hinges upon assessing the condition of the existing stand and seeding at the proper time.
items.summary:
This can be a cost-effective way to revitalize a diminishing stand or introduce legumes.

Timing is critical - frost seeding is typically done between mid-February and early March to coincide with the freeze-thaw cycle, which helps incorporate the seed into the soil. Seed should be applied to bare soil, not snow-covered ground.

The condition of the existing stand is also important. A thick thatch can hinder seed-to-soil contact, so it's recommended to closely graze or hay the area in the fall/winter before seeding. Bare spots are a good indicator that frost seeding may work well.

Soil type matters - frost seeding tends to be more successful on loam or clay soils that expand/contract during freeze-thaw, rather than sandy soils. Avoiding soil compaction by seeding when the ground is frozen is also important.

Adequate spring moisture is vital for establishing a healthy frost-seeded stand. While the potential benefits are high, timing, soil conditions, and moisture all play crucial roles in the success of frost seeding.

The article was authored by Dr. Shelby Gruss, an assistant professor and forage extension specialist at Iowa State University who joined the department in November 2023. Her research focuses on optimizing forage-based systems.

items.title: 7 Vegetables to Start From Seed in February
items.description: It takes a lot to get the farm ready for the growing season. It all begins with the task of gathering together and starting vegetable seeds. February is an ideal time to get many of your spring crops going. Consider these 7 vegetables as you prepare your rows. The post 7 Vegetables to Start From Seed in February appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Here are the key points:

1. February is a good time to start seeds indoors, using protected environments like greenhouses, cold frames, or low/high tunnels. This gives plants a head start before the outdoor growing season.

2. Slow-growing herbs like basil, oregano, and rosemary should be started in February, as they can take 1-4 weeks to germinate.

3. Tomatoes should be started in February, especially for growers in warmer regions. They take at least 80 days from seed to fruit.

4. Peppers are notoriously slow to germinate, taking up to a month. They also need 2-3 months to mature. Productive varieties include jalapeños, serranos, and shishitos.

5. Brassicas like broccoli, cabbage, kale, and cauliflower thrive in the cool spring weather. Leafy types grow quickly, while heading types take longer and may need winter protection.

6. Lettuce is easy to grow from seed in February and can handle light frosts. Leaf lettuces grow quickly, while heading types take more time.

7. Carrots and parsnips should be directly sown outdoors in February, as their taproots don't like being disturbed.

8. Onions and leeks should be planted from seed in February, as they take 75-140 days to mature.

The article emphasizes the importance of using protected growing environments like greenhouses, cold frames, and tunnels to get a head start on the growing season, even in cold climates.

items.description: You can also read the article in Portuguese and Spanish Introduction Recent dust storm events in central Illinois and across the Midwest have renewed attention on soil conservation, especially after the tragic May 2023 event near Springfield that caused an 80-vehicle pileup, eight fatalities, and dozens of injuries. These incidents highlight that soil loss is not only an agronomic issue but also a public safety and environmental concern. Reduced tillage and cover crops are well-established pract
items.summary:
Summarizing the key points from the agricultural news article:

The article reports on a 2-year project evaluating soybean performance in conservation agricultural systems in central Illinois and north-central Iowa. The study compared 4 management systems - conventional tillage (CT), fall strip-tillage (ST), no-tillage (NT), and no-tillage with a cereal rye cover crop (NT+CR) - each with 3 starter fertilizer strategies (unfertilized control, 15 lb N/ac, and 15 lb N/ac + 10 lb S/ac).

Key findings:
- Starter fertilizer increased early-season soybean biomass by 12% on average, but these early differences did not persist to later growth stages.
- Soybean yields ranged from 60-95 bu/ac across the 6 locations and 2 years, with no significant yield differences between tillage/cover crop systems.
- When accounting for operational costs, no-till had the highest partial net return, followed by strip-till and conventional tillage. No-till with cereal rye had the lowest partial net return due to higher cover crop management costs.

The project will continue in 2026 to track medium-term responses as the soil and residue dynamics change under the conservation systems. More data will be released once the trial is completed.

items.title: The February Greenhouse: What to Grow Now
items.description: When winter is halfway over, growing out of the elements is the only option for many farmers. Here, we share how to use a greenhouse to grow what the climate doesn’t allow and keep the revenue flowing. The post The February Greenhouse: What to Grow Now appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Greenhouses provide an enclosure that traps thermal heat, allowing for growing even when it's cold outside. 

Modular plastic greenhouses can raise temperatures up to 30 degrees higher, but require ventilation. Low tunnels and cold frames are simpler options that can raise temperatures 2-15 degrees. Larger, fortified greenhouses with climate controls allow for year-round growing.

Key crops to grow in February greenhouses include:
- Tomatoes and peppers, which benefit from the early start and consistent warmth and moisture
- Brassicas like kale, cabbage, cauliflower, and broccoli rabe, which can be protected from pests
- Lettuces, which can be grown earlier for spring markets
- Potatoes, to get a head start on full-sized or baby potatoes
- Onions, including sets, seeds, and bunching onions
- Flowers like lisianthus, coneflowers, and dahlias that take a long time to sprout

The article notes the importance of understanding the specific capabilities of your greenhouse setup to choose the best crops to grow. It advises using seed trays, heating mats, automatic lighting, and proper ventilation and climate control as needed.

items.title: Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land
items.description: Also called agroforestry, forest farming is a great way to work within your environmental parameters and utilize the tree canopy to produce more for your farm. Especially for those who live in forested areas, this practice enhances farm output without compromising the ecosystem. The post Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Originating in Brazil's tropical rainforests, this farming method takes advantage of the high productivity and biodiversity of forested areas.

The article outlines the benefits of forest farming, including:
- Improved water and soil quality, with tree roots holding more water and recharging groundwater.
- Carbon storage, with trees able to store up to 22 lbs of carbon per year in the first 20 years.
- Supporting diverse ecosystems of beneficial insects, birds, mammals, and fungi.
- Ability to grow specialty crops like mushrooms, ramps, syrups, and edible roots that thrive in forested environments.

The article advises that existing forested or riparian areas on a farm are ideal for implementing an agroforestry system. It recommends consulting local agricultural extension offices to develop a forest management plan and understand market opportunities for forest-grown crops.

Considerations include managing invasive tree species, understanding regulations around wild plant harvesting, and exploring various sales channels like online, agritourism, and direct-to-consumer options. The article emphasizes that forest farming does not need to be a large-scale operation and can benefit even small farms with some forested land.

Overall, the article presents forest farming as an ecological and economically viable option for farmers looking to diversify their operations and integrate their land into the surrounding landscape.

items.title: Getting Started with Spray Drones in Iowa: A Practical Guide

items.summary:
When used appropriately, spray drones can provide flexibility for timely applications, reduce field traffic, and improve access to difficult areas. However, adopting this technology requires careful consideration of regulations, training, insurance, and management practices.

- Farmers are encouraged to start on a limited scale, compare to conventional methods, and develop efficient procedures.
- Educational resources are available from Iowa State University, IDALS, and equipment dealers.
- Ongoing advancements in payload, automation, and integration with precision ag are expected.

The article provides a comprehensive guide for Iowa farmers to evaluate and adopt spray drone technology responsibly and effectively.

items.title: The 9 Best Flowers and Vegetables to Winter Sow
items.description: For farms in colder areas, starting seeds in time for the spring market requires a significant amount of time and indoor space. Winter sowing is a method that can be done outdoors and gives seedlings a stronger constitution as they mature. Here, we share plants that thrive when winter sown. The post The 9 Best Flowers and Vegetables to Winter Sow appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
It involves sowing seeds in reused containers like milk jugs or plastic bags and placing them outdoors to benefit from cold, moist winter conditions.

The best vegetables for winter sowing include hardy greens like kale, cabbage, and spinach. Cabbages come in standard and specialty varieties like Napa and 'Carex' with shorter maturation. Spinach varieties like 'Avon' and 'Space' resist mildew and bolting. Onions, especially long-day, short-day, and intermediate-day types, also do well when winter sown. Other great options are leafy greens like kale, collards, chard, and microgreens.

For flowers, perennials that need cold stratification are ideal, such as pansies, echinacea, snapdragons, larkspur, and scabiosa. Pansies provide early spring blooms, while echinacea, snapdragons, larkspur, and scabiosa attract beneficial insects.

The article emphasizes that winter sowing allows growers to maximize spring profits and productivity by getting a head start on hardy crops. It provides all the benefits of direct sowing with less risk to sensitive seedlings.

Despite declines in corn and soybean prices from mid-June to mid-July — Eastern Corn Belt cash prices fell 11% and 5%, respectively — farmer sentiment improved in July. Responses to the individual questi
items.summary:
Key points:

- Farmer sentiment improved in July 2024, with the Purdue/CME Group Ag Economy Barometer index rising 8 points to 113.

- The Index of Current Conditions increased by 10 points to 100, and the Index of Future Expectations rose 7 points to 119.

- Despite declines in corn and soybean prices (11% and 5% respectively), sentiment improved due to fewer respondents reporting worsened conditions and lower expectations of negative future outcomes.

- The top concerns for farmers were high input costs (34%), risk of lower crop/livestock prices (29%), and rising interest rates (17%, down from 23% in June).

- The Farm Financial Performance Index dropped 4 points to 81, 6 points lower than July 2023, reflecting worries about weakening commodity prices and high input costs.

- The Farm Capital Investment Index rose 6 points to 38, though it remains 7 points lower than July 2023, as fewer producers believe it's a bad time to make large investments.

- The Short-Term Farmland Value Expectations Index rose to 118, while the Long-Term Index dropped 6 points to 146, with fewer farmers expecting values to rise over the next five years.

- 72% of crop farmers expect cash rental rates to remain roughly the same as 2024, with 15% anticipating an increase and 13% expecting a decrease.

items.title: Purdue researchers adopt interdisciplinary approach to assessing emerging tar spot disease in corn
items.description: For more than a century, tar spot fungal disease in corn kept its distance from the U.S., biding its time
items.summary:
Purdue researchers are taking an interdisciplinary approach to assess the emerging tar spot disease in corn:

- Tar spot, a fungal disease, was first detected in the U.S. in 2015 and has since spread to 16 states and Ontario, Canada. It has also affected crops in 15 other countries.

- The research team, led by C.D. Cruz, associate professor of botany and plant pathology at Purdue, is using a mix of statistical, data science, epidemiology, microbiology, artificial intelligence, and computer vision methods to better understand the dynamics of tar spot.

- The work is funded by two USDA grants totaling nearly $1.1 million. Collaborators include researchers from Colombia, Mexico, Ecuador, South Korea, and the U.S.

- Previous efforts include developing a digital method for quantifying tar spot using an algorithm called SCDA, which was tested against human raters. Ongoing work aims to improve the model's accuracy.

- Another research effort involves a collaboration between the agricultural and engineering teams, led by Mohammad Jahanshahi, to adapt computer vision and AI approaches from civil infrastructure monitoring to detect and classify crop disease symptoms.

- The team is also working on quantifying and modeling tar spot epidemics in production-style fields, using disease observations and drone-based imagery.

- The interdisciplinary approach aims to provide rapid and accurate information to stakeholders, addressing the urgent need to address biosecurity challenges with a science-based approach.

The publication covers key potassium concepts, including the sources of potassium, how it moves through the soil-plant system, and the factors that influence potassium availability and uptake by crops.

items.title: Questions to consider prior to replanting a soybean field
items.description: Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist, UW-Madison Early in the growing season, abiotic (freezing temperatures, hail, flooding, etc.) and biotic (slugs, deer, disease, insects, etc.) factors often reduce soybean plant stands. A soybean …
items.summary:
Key points:

- Abiotic (e.g. freezing, hail, flooding) and biotic (e.g. slugs, deer, disease, insects) factors can reduce soybean plant stands early in the growing season.

- When plant stands are below the recommended 100,000-120,000 plants per acre, farmers should evaluate whether to replant.

- Factors to consider include: remaining plant population, growth stage, soil moisture, planting date, weed pressure, and yield potential.

- Replanting soybeans after June 1 in Wisconsin may result in a 0.5-1 bushel/acre yield reduction per day.

- Soybean yields can be maintained with plant stands as low as 75,000 plants/acre if the remaining plants are healthy and evenly distributed.

- Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist at UW-Madison, advises farmers to carefully evaluate their specific situation before deciding to replant.

The article provides guidance to help farmers make an informed decision on whether to replant their soybean fields based on various agronomic and economic factors.
